title: The Rainbow of Why, Go Jackson Pollock with Those Colors
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Building on the Caroline Ong "math is beautiful" example, Stuart introduces his Rainbow of Why framework, a palette of research-backed reasons students come to value a subject, through the unlikely lens of Jackson Pollock's action paintings. He argues that Pollock's work is bold, counter-cultural, energetic, and made on the fly, and that value-building in the classroom should carry the same qualities rather than feeling like a rote obligation. His central critique is that American education overuses just two colors on the palette, utility and personal relevance, training students toward an unhelpfully self-focused view of why learning matters, at the expense of other legitimate reasons like purpose or intrinsic beauty. He credits Utah educator Doug Anderson with coining the Rainbow of Why phrase and notes the concept receives a full chapter in his book The Will to Learn. The piece closes by urging teachers to treat Value-cultivation as creative, exploratory work, a joy, not a job.
points: Stuart names a specific pedagogical failure mode: American classrooms over-rely on utility and personal relevance as reasons-to-value, crowding out other legitimate motivators.
The Jackson Pollock analogy argues that effective value-communication should be bold, counter-cultural, and improvisational rather than formulaic.
He credits the Rainbow of Why concept to Utah educator Doug Anderson, situating the framework within a broader professional community rather than claiming sole authorship.
Value cultivation is explicitly reframed as creative and exploratory work rather than an obligatory classroom-management task.
quotes: I labeled this as an example of a strategy we're currently contemplating: An Apologist Winsome and Sure. They mean a LOT to me in the realm of cultivating student motivation. A LOT.
It's counter-cultural — this thing was made in 1949, about the same time cookie-cutter communities like Levittown were becoming popular. It's energetic.
You'll move students best toward Value when you intentionally use all the colors. In American education, we tend to paint way too frequently with utility.
This is a painter's palette for a reason — I want you to view Value cultivation as a creative work, an exploratory work, a beautiful work; not a have-to, a get-to; not a job, but rather a joy.
And finally, I want you to paint with these colors like Jackson Pollock; be bold, be counter-cultural, be energetic, be okay with "on-the-fly" action painting.
